patient_descriptions.attribution: patient_retrospective; causal interpretations in text belong to author
patient_descriptions.quoted_text: * cognitive dysfunction (“brain fog”) at all times: IQ reduction (ca. -2SD), extreme forgetfulness, trouble finding words, trouble constructing complex mental models/abstractions, reduced mental imagery (aphantasia)

patient_descriptions.attribution: Patient’s retained message. Date is the report date.
patient_descriptions.quoted_text:
re brainfog, might be important to emphasize: baseline lack of clarity of mind, slower thinking, bad memory (trouble finding words eg), slight derealization etc, but when i exert myself, the more i go the worse it gets – it's a linear increase in real time. when i don't do anything it usually stays at the baseline. if i really overdo it, i have the extremely painful paralyzing brain burns [when i just curl up and wait for it motionless to pass].

i thought this might be important because the severity is not constant, suggesting it's not permanent damage but likely bad circulation (hypoperfusion).

aliases: Distinct deep muscle fatigue described after NADH

patient_descriptions.attribution: Patient’s retained message. Date is the report date.
patient_descriptions.quoted_text: tbf i was paralyzed before when the brain burning was so painful i didn't think i could move, but if i forced myself i could, so i suspect it was my brain trying to protect myself. however the new thing now is that i feel this paralysis more directly in the muscles

patient_descriptions.attribution: Patient’s retained message. Date is the report date.
patient_descriptions.quoted_text: oh and this time i felt it also when my brain wasn't burning, unlike before, so it seems to be independent now, whereas before i only had paralysis like events when my brain was "on fire" and more an action paralysis, and this time proper muscle fatigue

* GI issues:
* orange diarrhea for a few days, then a few days of constipation
* near constant gut pain in one or the other or both colic flexures
* especially strong and sharp after sulfur-rich foods, eg. onions (later confirmed sulfur-reducing species overgrowth)
* for some time had green diarrhea + liver/pancreas pain and elevated enzymes → mostly resolved
* gall spasms with fat intake → now slowly tapering up fat again

annotations:ANN-S3-521.qualification: Undated retrospective attribution. Interpretation is attributed to the researcher in the retrospective history.
annotations:ANN-S3-521.summary:
* Research group’s OAT evaluation - hypothesis:
* Candida overgrowth indicated by elevated 3-oxoglutarate (3) and arabinose (7)
* Succinate/fumarate/malate (24/25/26) are all increased in relation to 2-oxoglutarate/aconitate/citrate (27/28/29). There likely is 'theft' of isocitrate by Candida, shifting the Krebs cycle.
* Mitochondrial dysfunction suggested by high 3-hydroxyglutaric (31), which might be cause by lead or mercury exposure.
* Altered β-oxidation markers (suberic/sebacic), and mild ketosis
* Glutathione stress due to NAC/C imbalance and cysteine “theft” by candida-derived acetaldehyde, reducing detox capacity
* Dopamine and serotonin metabolism issues from aldehyde dehydrogenase inhibition (acetaldehyde), impacting neurotransmitter balance
* Elevated phosphoric acid possibly due to metabolic or endocrine dysregulation or kidneys, not diet
* High B5 and low B6 activity indicate cofactor imbalances; consider P5P supplementation
* Potential carnitine deficiency impacting β-oxidation; L-carnitine may help
* H2S-producing microbes may impair autophagy and mitochondrial renewal

annotations:ANN-S3-575.qualification: Undated retrospective attribution. Interpretation is attributed to the researcher in the retrospective history.
annotations:ANN-S3-575.summary:
* Research group’s biomesight evaluation - hypothesis:
* Hydrogen Sulfide Overproduction: Elevated Bilophila wadsworthia suggests excess H₂S production, contributing to gut dysbiosis and inflammation.
* Leaky Gut & Inflammation: Increased gut permeability likely leads to endotoxemia and systemic inflammation, affecting brain function via cytokines, GDF15, mast cell activation, and urea cycle dysfunction.
* Severely Low Beneficial Bacteria:
* Bifidobacterium, Lactobacillus, Faecalibacterium, and Roseburia are depleted, impairing gut barrier integrity and butyrate production.
* High Akkermansia: Unusually elevated Akkermansia muciniphila may degrade the gut mucus barrier, increasing LPS-driven inflammation.
* Elevated Bacteroides: High Bacteroides could contribute to metabolic and inflammatory dysregulation.
* Oxalate Degradation Impaired: Low Oxalobacter may contribute to oxalate accumulation and food intolerance.
* Transsulfuration Dysfunction & Glutathione Deficiency
* Cysteine Metabolism & H₂S Link:
* Cysteine supplementation improved symptoms (e.g., tinnitus reversal), suggesting prior deficiency.
* However, cysteine fuels Bilophila and worsens H₂S overproduction, potentially causing GI symptoms.
* Glutathione Deficiency: OAT analysis suggests glutathione depletion, reinforcing transsulfuration dysfunction suspicion.
* Cysteine is the rate-limiting substrate for glutathione synthesis, but excess H₂S inhibits cystathionine gamma-lyase (CGL), impairing conversion to glutathione.
* Reduced glutathione production exacerbates oxidative stress and inflammation.
* Transsulfuration-Impaired Inflammation Resolution:
* H₂S normally promotes glutathione synthesis at low levels but inhibits it at high concentrations.
* Mitochondrial dysfunction and ROS-driven cysteine depletion further disrupt glutathione availability, worsening oxidative stress and inflammatory signaling.

archive_findings:S1-F2480-1.summary: Late October 2024 decline into severe weakness and near paralysis after reported excess NADH preparation with magnesium exposure. Stopped NADH. On November 2 still mostly in bed; a computer session preceded about two hours of near paralysis. By November 12 reported no longer bedridden after resuming vitamins. Patient considered progression an alternative explanation. The S5 calendar diary dates NADH initiation to the evening of October 21, 2024, excess NADH to October 22, and the first documented physical crash to October 23. Magnesium followed NADH by about five hours. The exact onset across the night of October 22–23 is unresolved. The clinician identifies the October 23 “magnesium poisoning” entry as new deep muscle fatigue. The October 25 account describes progressive sleepiness and weakness, unusually good sleep, near-paralysis the next day, muscle cramps, and tingling without the usual pains. On November 2 the patient explicitly contrasted prior movement limitation during brain burning with fatigue now felt directly in the muscles, including when the brain burning was absent.

archive_messages:S1-M1617.text: The patient described severe neurological symptoms despite working with a clinical team. Gut symptoms had partly improved from constant pain and one bowel movement per week. Energy had improved, deep sleep had increased from about 20 minutes to 45–90 minutes, and testosterone had risen from the low end of the range. Brain fog and POTS persisted. He described a nonliposomal experimental nanocarrier formulation and relayed the developers’ claim that it could increase absorption of substances taken alongside it. He took a slightly larger than intended dose of the NADH formulation, then his usual magnesium dose about five hours later. He recalled a roughly 12-hour steady-state interval for the formulation. He became progressively sleepy and weak, slept unusually well, and felt effectively paralysed the next day. He had muscle cramps and tingling, without his usual pains and other symptoms. He called this magnesium toxicity but also considered an acute ME-related change. Symptoms began clearing as he drank large amounts of water. The team was considering a formulation intended to target the blood–brain barrier. He was considering switching to off-label trials if their experiments failed and was avoiding concurrent drugs because of the proposed absorption interaction.

high-level and incomplete list of hypotheses on neuro LC that i shared with someone recently:
- hypoperfusion: low blood oxygen supply due to impaired circulation. this can be for a few reasons: vascular inflammation induced dilation failure, nervous system damage/inflammation caused dysautonomia, AABs causing vagus nerve dysfunction, etc
- pierced BBB: fibrin clots, leukocytes, histamine inducing particles etc leaking into the brain
- viral persistence in brain
- last 2 points would both cause persistent glial activation -> chronic neuroinflammation
- damage of specific brain regions causing different abnormalities: brain stem -> dysautonomia, pituitary gland -> (hypocortisolemia, hypothryoidism, etc), cortex -> direct neurological symptoms, etc
- general demyelination
- pierced blood-CSF barrier, CSF reservoirs
- and of course the brain would enter some form of hypometabolism under duress like hypoxia and inflammation, although i can imagine that could happen due to other reasons too

most of my blood work has returned normal, except for my cellular immune status:

- slightly elevated IgE (25% above lab defined upper limit), rest of immunoglobulins normal, suggesting some form of MCAS still an issue
- low end of CD3+CD4+ T helper cell range, suggesting exhaustion
- CD4/CD8 ratio: 1.2
- suboptimal CD3+HLA-DR+ T cell activation, suggesting exhastion
- suboptimal hybrid NKT cell levels
- low end of CD19+ B cell level
- excessive CD16+CD56dim NK cell level – indicates an active immune response, chronic infection, or immune dysregulation

- suboptimal NK cell function – despite elevated NK cell counts, this suggests an ineffective and exhausted immune response, chronic inflammation

To explain nSMase2 briefly-

Cancer cells make exosomes with pro-inflammatory factors in, so they are essentially bombarding each other and bystander immune cells with these pro-inflammatory factors all the time. This actually makes the cancer cells resistant to being killed

nSMase2 controls exosome production. Inhibit it, the cancerous cells produce less exosomes and become more sensitised to being killed

Gut/liver/brain axis gets messed up;

Can be gut dysbiosis -> endotoxemia, MCAS -> brainstem inflammation. The area postrema (in brainstem) is the only part of brain outside blood-brain barrier; it gets information on inflammatory and metabolic processes and relays that to the solitary tract. The area postrema can be full of mast cells in neurological disorders, including ME

archive_messages:S1-M55.text: The researcher interpreted this cytokine panel as weighted toward Th2 signalling (IL-4/IL-13), connected this with IgE and suspected MCAS, mentioned omalizumab or alternative approaches, and asked how well antihistamines controlled symptoms.

archive_messages:S1-M553.text:
The gut can mostly be fine, and metabolic issues are the major problem; the area postrema also responds to incretins like GLP-1/GIP/glucagon. If metabolic issues get out of hand, the liver becomes mildly insufficient - especially important if urea cycle is impaired. Urea cycle is impaired by mast cells, so also important in previous example; loss of urea cycle components due to TCA cycle problems is also contributing

This pressures the brain itself as there is more toxic ammonia in CNS and glutamine production from glutamate and ammonia

- other physical activities 
- cognitive exertion: reading, complicated music, fast scenes in a movie, talking, listening to or just thinking about complex concepts

archive_messages:S1-M857.text: thank you! been meaning to check up on my gut. also want to see if there are any parasites

archive_messages:S1-M860.text: Ah, keep remembering stuff - if you aren't taking high dose thiamine, that is a good shout, especially if you get the feeling of increased intracranial pressure and visual symptoms (double vision especially) that come with that

archive_messages:S1-M861.text: as in, i should take it?

archive_messages:S1-M862.text: Starting low dose is recommended as can cause metabolism to worsen (acidosis) in a very unlucky few

archive_messages:S1-M865.text: From 100mg up to 2 grams a day

archive_messages:S1-M867.text: There will be like 10mg in your b complex probably

archive_messages:S1-M868.text: Generally recommended to start at 100mg thiamine/50mg benfotiamine/10mg TTFD (aka fursultiamine) and go up towards 1g/500mg/100mg respectively

archive_messages:S1-M869.text: High dose thiamine may reduce brain swelling by regulating carbonic anhydrase, which is targeted by diamox (acetazolamide), the drug they use in hospitals to reduce ICP

archive_messages:S1-M871.text: although 10% of 1g is still 100mg so likely not coming close either way

archive_messages:S1-M872.text: is the brain swollen in lc/me? i had done one MRI and they hadn't found structural changes but that was only about 2 months in

archive_messages:S1-M876.text: how similar are ME and LC?

archive_messages:S1-M877.text: some are saying it's the exact same disease

archive_messages:S1-M879.text: ME and classical neuro-LC both sit on the same 'spectrum' of disease entities. Chronic stressor fries mineral stores/immune system, maybe gut and liver, maybe vagus or other major nerves are infected with herpesviruses also - hypothalamus and brainstem get inflamed and malfunction due to external factors and potential direct infection by covid/HHV-6/Coxsackies/Echoviruses

archive_messages:S1-M880.text: But as you can see, ME/LC are not well defined entities at all

archive_messages:S1-M881.text: yeah that's my gripe i guess. they serve more as a category of dysfunctions

archive_messages:S1-M884.text: also what coinfections should one always test for other than the ones just mentioned?

archive_messages:S1-M885.text: i haven't checked hhv hsv coxsackie entero echo yet

archive_messages:S1-M886.text: This is why I keep on talking about subtyping, we can do some real work when we understand what separate pathologies are at play in each major group of patients/understand rare pathologies in respect to genetic data

archive_messages:S1-M894.text: so more of a symptom or nth order effect then?

archive_messages:S1-M900.text: I think it is an interplay between immune system hyperactivity and immunodeficiency

archive_messages:S1-M902.text: Or there is immunodeficiency which does not impact NETs formation, chronic infection takes hold and NET threshold is released w/ inflammation induced loss of tolerance -> disease initation

archive_messages:S1-M909.text: Many with LC w/EBV reactivation have lupus-like LC, which is again another phenotype I think is clearly defined

archive_messages:S1-M925.text: here's the probiotic i'm taking. contains prebiotic in the form of inulin

archive_messages:S1-M930.text: There is a probiotic people are taking recently called Lactobacillus fermentum ME-3. Supposedly it makes glutathione

archive_messages:S1-M934.text: oh yeah, many are having glutathione deficiencies. likely the oxidative stress exhausts stores. want to test that too

archive_messages:S1-M938.text: i wonder if that's because of viral persistence in there or just higher concentration of dysregulated immune cells

archive_messages:S1-M9399.text: We need to improve gut slowly over a period of time. There is no quick fix for that unfortunately

archive_messages:S1-M94.text: to be clear, most issues in LC can be explained away with the macrophage-endothelial induced cascade, I just think that there are other pathways too, and many of these theories fail to account for the fact that these different pathways feed back into each other –– systems/chaos theory understanding is needed here, as you are well aware.

baseline_states:BL-09.description: On November 2 he reported that sitting up to research and watch a series two days earlier preceded another two-hour episode. By the report he felt better but remained below his former level, resting all day. Cognitive exertion brought on symptoms sooner.
baseline_states:BL-09.interpretation_limit: The episode duration refers to near-paralysis. Rest after it was partly deliberate.

baseline_states:BL-10.date_basis: observations on Nov 9/12/15 and Dec 4/7; interval not continuously sampled
baseline_states:BL-10.description: By November 9 he was no longer bedridden, although still severely fogged. On November 12 he reiterated the mobility improvement and perceived benefit after resuming vitamins. On January 8 he recalled roughly two weeks bedridden, two weeks back at baseline without PEM, then another decline. A November 15 hospital trip provoked several hours of symptoms. On December 4 he felt roughly at his own baseline, and on December 7 could walk without dizziness while brain burning had subsided.
baseline_states:BL-10.interpretation_limit: The December comparator is his own baseline at the time. Persistent brain fog and exertional flares complicate any claim of complete recovery or permanent loss from NADH alone.
baseline_states:BL-10.title: No longer bedridden; intermittent near-baseline mobility

baseline_states:BL-S5-POST-NADH.description: NADH was taken October 20–21 and restarted October 25–28, 2024, according to the reviewer. New deep muscle fatigue and a major crash were first documented October 23. Marked weakness and confinement to bed recurred October 29. The patient attributed a major baseline drop to NADH. November records describe partial recovery followed by a later relapse. Magnesium and exertion were also discussed. The October 25 account describes progressive sleepiness and weakness, unusually good sleep, near-paralysis the next day, muscle cramps, and tingling without the usual pains. On November 2 the patient explicitly contrasted prior movement limitation during brain burning with fatigue now felt directly in the muscles, including when the brain burning was absent. Daily overall ratings were 5/10 on October 21–22, 2/10 on October 23, and 3–4/10 through October 28. On October 29 he woke with numb or weak arms, especially around the shoulders and hands, and needed about an hour to get up. The clinician identifies this as the new deep muscle-fatigue phenotype. Later that day he felt tranquilized and confined to bed. Moving his limbs took considerable effort but remained possible. Muscle symptoms then eased and PENE followed. The diary also records suspected overexertion the previous evening.

historical_entries:S3:chronology:502.subject: (Oct 22-29) slow-release NADH formula at first caused rapid improvement in symptoms, but after 3 days caused a major crash → PEM symptom first appears here → permanently lowered baseline ever since:
historical_entries:S3:chronology:502.text:
* (Oct 22-29) slow-release NADH formula at first caused rapid improvement in symptoms, but after 3 days caused a major crash → PEM symptom first appears here → permanently lowered baseline ever since:
* Oct 22-25: first three days, improvement
* Oct 25: major paralysis, but no other symptoms. at first we thought it was due to magnesium toxicity since I had taken the previous night’s NADH dose rather close to my evening magnesium
* Oct 25-27: two day rest
* Oct 28-29: resume NADH, crash badly on 29th, this time not only muscle fatigue but a host of new symptoms, see below
* up until this point biggest symptom was ‘brain burns’ which, while debilitating, was manageable → now often spend all day in bed in dark room unable to do anything
* hyopthesis: issue in mitochondrial electron transport chain complex I
* hyopthesis: NADH/NAD+ ratio shift changes Krebs cycle enzymes

historical_entries:S3:chronology:521.subject: Research group’s OAT evaluation - hypothesis:
historical_entries:S3:chronology:521.text:
* Research group’s OAT evaluation - hypothesis:
* Candida overgrowth indicated by elevated 3-oxoglutarate (3) and arabinose (7)
* Succinate/fumarate/malate (24/25/26) are all increased in relation to 2-oxoglutarate/aconitate/citrate (27/28/29). There likely is 'theft' of isocitrate by Candida, shifting the Krebs cycle.
* Mitochondrial dysfunction suggested by high 3-hydroxyglutaric (31), which might be cause by lead or mercury exposure.
* Altered β-oxidation markers (suberic/sebacic), and mild ketosis
* Glutathione stress due to NAC/C imbalance and cysteine “theft” by candida-derived acetaldehyde, reducing detox capacity
* Dopamine and serotonin metabolism issues from aldehyde dehydrogenase inhibition (acetaldehyde), impacting neurotransmitter balance
* Elevated phosphoric acid possibly due to metabolic or endocrine dysregulation or kidneys, not diet
* High B5 and low B6 activity indicate cofactor imbalances; consider P5P supplementation
* Potential carnitine deficiency impacting β-oxidation; L-carnitine may help
* H2S-producing microbes may impair autophagy and mitochondrial renewal

historical_entries:S3:chronology:575.subject: Research group’s biomesight evaluation - hypothesis:
historical_entries:S3:chronology:575.text:
* Research group’s biomesight evaluation - hypothesis:
* Hydrogen Sulfide Overproduction: Elevated Bilophila wadsworthia suggests excess H₂S production, contributing to gut dysbiosis and inflammation.
* Leaky Gut & Inflammation: Increased gut permeability likely leads to endotoxemia and systemic inflammation, affecting brain function via cytokines, GDF15, mast cell activation, and urea cycle dysfunction.
* Severely Low Beneficial Bacteria:
* Bifidobacterium, Lactobacillus, Faecalibacterium, and Roseburia are depleted, impairing gut barrier integrity and butyrate production.
* High Akkermansia: Unusually elevated Akkermansia muciniphila may degrade the gut mucus barrier, increasing LPS-driven inflammation.
* Elevated Bacteroides: High Bacteroides could contribute to metabolic and inflammatory dysregulation.
* Oxalate Degradation Impaired: Low Oxalobacter may contribute to oxalate accumulation and food intolerance.
* Transsulfuration Dysfunction & Glutathione Deficiency
* Cysteine Metabolism & H₂S Link:
* Cysteine supplementation improved symptoms (e.g., tinnitus reversal), suggesting prior deficiency.
* However, cysteine fuels Bilophila and worsens H₂S overproduction, potentially causing GI symptoms.
* Glutathione Deficiency: OAT analysis suggests glutathione depletion, reinforcing transsulfuration dysfunction suspicion.
* Cysteine is the rate-limiting substrate for glutathione synthesis, but excess H₂S inhibits cystathionine gamma-lyase (CGL), impairing conversion to glutathione.
* Reduced glutathione production exacerbates oxidative stress and inflammation.
* Transsulfuration-Impaired Inflammation Resolution:
* H₂S normally promotes glutathione synthesis at low levels but inhibits it at high concentrations.
* Mitochondrial dysfunction and ROS-driven cysteine depletion further disrupt glutathione availability, worsening oxidative stress and inflammatory signaling.

historical_entries:S3:symptom:013.attribution: patient_retrospective; causal interpretations in text belong to author
historical_entries:S3:symptom:013.subject: Post Exertional Malaise (PEM):
historical_entries:S3:symptom:013.text:
* Post Exertional Malaise (PEM):
* exertion causes sudden shutdown of executive function, both cognitive and physical
* 1-3x/day, lasting a few hours, but sometimes recurring for days
* but it’s never a continuous crash even then
* progression: top of forearms/hands tingling (rapidly fluctuating, slightly corrosive, acid-like unpleasant sensation) → feet/calves tingling → nape tingling/pulsing → occipital lobe fatigue, pressures or sometimes headache → tranquilizing sensation and pulsing along spine → brain slows down suddenly (extreme CNS fatigue) → rarely almost full paralysis but usually just an intense malaise sensation (a bit like the flu), also tingling sometimes intensifies to a corrosion like pain → often narcoleptic sleep pressure, often fall asleep regardless of time of day
* not muscle fatigue!
* I can still move muscles, PEM seems to be in CNS with peripheral tingling as above, but if it’s very strong my “willpower” to move is zero
* unless in severe crash, eating immediately lifts all symptoms (including sleep pressure), sometimes as soon as the first bite
* Herxheimer reaction crashes are particularly violent, tingling is far more painful/corrosive
* “evening PEM”: every day starting 5-6pm, getting at least initial parts of above progression (ie at least tingling) → IL-1beta circadian upregulation?

reconciliations:Q-014.alternate_or_limitation: Previous reconstruction: The patient reported on October 26 that NADH had been resumed the previous night. On October 29 he described being stuck in bed and weak. On October 30 he confirmed he had stopped. The precise last dose is unknown. He reported he was no longer bedridden on November 9 and 12 and described being close to his own baseline on December 4. January 8 recollection describes a subsequent relapse. The retrospective history places the restart on October 28 after a two-day break and attributes a permanent drop to NADH. The contemporaneous messages support an earlier restart and document recovery and relapse. The initial dose and contributions of NADH, magnesium, exertion and concurrent changes are uncertain.
reconciliations:Q-014.subject: October NADH restart and recovery
reconciliations:Q-014.working_interpretation: The reviewer dates the restarted course October 25–28 inclusive. The October 26 message refers to the previous night; the patient reported being off NADH by October 30. Subsequent improvement and relapse remain documented.

reconciliations:Q-NADH-PHENOTYPE.alternate_or_limitation: S6 clarifies phenotype. Retrospective reports supply additional symptoms. Magnesium poisoning was a patient hypothesis. Exact dose and mechanism remain uncertain. S3:symptom:013 separately describes later CNS shutdown without muscle fatigue.
reconciliations:Q-NADH-PHENOTYPE.subject: Pre-NADH neurological/PENE versus new post-NADH deep muscle fatigue
reconciliations:Q-NADH-PHENOTYPE.working_interpretation: The clinician identified the pre-NADH crashes as neurological PENE or brain-burning episodes. Pain could limit movement or speech. The diary also contains generic lack-of-strength ratings. The distinctive deep muscle fatigue and physical PEM first appeared after NADH. The clinician identifies the October 23 “magnesium poisoning” entry as new deep muscle fatigue. The October 25 account describes progressive sleepiness and weakness, unusually good sleep, near-paralysis the next day, muscle cramps, and tingling without the usual pains. On November 2 the patient explicitly contrasted prior movement limitation during brain burning with fatigue now felt directly in the muscles, including when the brain burning was absent.

reconciliations:Q-S5-NADH-START.alternate_or_limitation: Previous reconstruction: The S5 calendar diary dates NADH initiation to the evening of October 21, 2024, excess NADH to October 22, and the first documented physical crash to October 23. Magnesium followed NADH by about five hours. The exact onset across the night of October 22–23 is unresolved. S6 clarifies phenotype. Retrospective reports supply additional symptoms. Magnesium poisoning was a patient hypothesis. Exact dose and mechanism remain uncertain. S3:symptom:013 separately describes later CNS shutdown without muscle fatigue. S5 does not name a restart. S1-M1899 supports an inferred October 25 night restart. The later S3 account places it October 28–29. An October 23 all-lipo hold does not specify NADH.

s1_reported_course:S1-M1617#1.account: The patient described severe neurological symptoms despite working with a clinical team. Gut symptoms had partly improved from constant pain and one bowel movement per week. Energy had improved, deep sleep had increased from about 20 minutes to 45–90 minutes, and testosterone had risen from the low end of the range. Brain fog and POTS persisted. He described a nonliposomal experimental nanocarrier formulation and relayed the developers’ claim that it could increase absorption of substances taken alongside it. He took a slightly larger than intended dose of the NADH formulation, then his usual magnesium dose about five hours later. He recalled a roughly 12-hour steady-state interval for the formulation. He became progressively sleepy and weak, slept unusually well, and felt effectively paralysed the next day. He had muscle cramps and tingling, without his usual pains and other symptoms. He called this magnesium toxicity but also considered an acute ME-related change. Symptoms began clearing as he drank large amounts of water. The team was considering a formulation intended to target the blood–brain barrier. He was considering switching to off-label trials if their experiments failed and was avoiding concurrent drugs because of the proposed absorption interaction.

source_lines:S3:504.text: * Oct 25: major paralysis, but no other symptoms. at first we thought it was due to magnesium toxicity since I had taken the previous night’s NADH dose rather close to my evening magnesium

source_lines:S3:506.text: * Oct 28-29: resume NADH, crash badly on 29th, this time not only muscle fatigue but a host of new symptoms, see below

source_lines:S3:507.text: * up until this point biggest symptom was ‘brain burns’ which, while debilitating, was manageable → now often spend all day in bed in dark room unable to do anything

source_lines:S3:508.text: * hyopthesis: issue in mitochondrial electron transport chain complex I

source_lines:S3:657.text: * Lyme test: a Lyme specialist tested via Western blot → Borrelia negative

I hypothesized that THC had been synthesized from the hemp. This was the patient's hypothesis. The episode lasted two hours and I could not move or speak. A small amount of black stool in the morning and evening was attributed by the patient to alginite. Strong abdominal pain before the evening bowel movement resolved afterward. [V15]
